title: Fully polynomial learning of halfspace intersections under Gaussian and uniform inputs
formal: Resolve the following two distribution-specific questions, separately. For \(D_n=\gamma_n=N(0,I_n)\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and for \(D_n=U_n\), the uniform measure on \(\{-1,+1\}^n\), does there exist a uniform randomized learner \(A_D\) and constants \(B_D,C_D\ge1\) such that, for all integers \(n,k\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and all intersections \(f\) of at most \(k\) affine halfspaces, \(A_D(n,k,t)\), using only independent examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D_n\), outputs a predictor \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr\!\left[\Pr_{x\sim D_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23\] in total training, output-writing and evaluation cost at most \(B_D(n+k+t)^{C_D}\)? The Gaussian branch uses the explicit real-arithmetic convention below; the Boolean-cube branch uses bit computation. The learner may be improper. Both the number of halfspaces and inverse accuracy are variable parameters: a polynomial whose exponent depends on \(k\) or \(t\) does not answer either branch affirmatively. A full resolution reports an answer to each branch, rather than treating failure of one as a classification of both.

source_formulation.text: Can intersections of a variable number of halfspaces be learned in time polynomial in dimension, number of halfspaces and inverse accuracy under Gaussian inputs or uniform Boolean-cube inputs?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

why: Simple independent input coordinates do not identify which inequality caused a negative label. The question asks whether that ambiguity creates a computational barrier even when the distribution is completely known. Its uniform dependence on the number of inequalities and desired accuracy separates practical polynomial learning from algorithms efficient only for fixed parameters.
status_note: The 2025 selected paragraph asks about Gaussian and uniform Boolean-cube inputs; the main factorizable two-margin-halfspace theorem is a different setting. Through 16 September 2026, the checked primary results include Alman–Patel–Servedio’s subexponential distribution-free learner (v2, July), bounded-geometric-width Gaussian learning applications, and a proper agnostic Gaussian learner with nonconstant parameter-dependent exponents. None supplies a checked fully polynomial answer for both source questions. This is an uncertain current-status assessment, not a proof of openness. The Gaussian exact-real convention and discrete bit convention are explicit; a theorem in a different cost model requires a justified transfer.

importance.reason: A central distribution-specific learning problem for conjunctions of linear thresholds, connecting geometric prediction and Boolean learning; both variable intersection size and inverse accuracy are essential to the unresolved efficiency target.

sentences: The card asks separately whether intersections of a variable number of affine halfspaces can be learned efficiently under Gaussian and uniform Boolean-cube inputs.
The desired polynomial bounds cover dimension, intersection size, inverse accuracy, training and prediction.
Labels come only from independent noiseless examples, and the output predictor may lie outside the target class.
The surrounding margin theorem and newer subexponential, bounded-width and proper-learning results do not supply the requested uniform polynomial guarantee.
A Lean resolution must prove or refute the full learner-existence statement in each explicitly defined computational model.

definitions:
An affine halfspace has Boolean value \(+1\) when \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i+b\ge0\), and value \(-1\) otherwise, for arbitrary real \(w_1,\ldots,w_n,b\). Its boundary is included in the positive side. An intersection has value \(+1\) exactly when all its component inequalities hold; otherwise it has value \(-1\). The intersection with no components is the constant positive function. All coefficients and the number of nonredundant inequalities are hidden; only the upper bound \(k\) is supplied. No coefficient-size, margin, balance or homogeneity promise is added. On the cube, the function is simply the restriction of those inequalities to the finite domain; their real coefficients are not input strings whose sizes the learner must read.

\(\gamma_n\) has independent standard normal coordinates, with joint density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\). Under \(U_n\), each of the \(2^n\) sign vectors has mass \(2^{-n}\). The appropriate distribution is known to its learner, but the target is unknown. Each example is an independent draw with the exact noiseless target label. The learner cannot ask for labels at chosen points, inspect the target description, or query conditional distributions. The inner probability is disagreement on a fresh example; the outer probability includes training examples and the learner’s random coins. The error tolerance is \(\varepsilon=1/t\), with integer \(t\) supplied in unary together with \(n,k\). These reciprocal tolerances define arbitrary requested accuracy up to a constant factor without introducing an uncounted rational encoding length. Confidence is fixed at \(2/3\); neither branch promises perfect recovery of coefficients.

For the cube, \(A_U\) is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a source of independent fair bits and an example tape. Writing a labeled example costs \(n+1\) bit operations. The output is an ordinary finite acyclic Boolean circuit, using AND, OR and NOT gates and constants, evaluated on the input signs encoded as bits. Training, reading, output length, and worst-case output evaluation time are all counted. The polynomial bound must hold on every sample and coin history. The same program and constants must work for every \(n,k,t,f\), with no advice depending on input length.

For the Gaussian branch, use one finite real-register program whose fixed constants are rational. Copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division with an explicit zero-denominator guard, comparison, branching, and generating a fair bit have unit cost; discrete control, register access and output writing are also charged. Loading one exact labeled Gaussian vector costs \(n+1\) units. Integer control and the unary public parameters do not supply any infinite advice. There is no floor or digit extraction, optimization oracle, expectation oracle or oracle deciding general real-number properties. The output is a finite acyclic arithmetic-and-comparison circuit with constants computed during training and a total Boolean sign output. Every division must be guarded so evaluation is defined on every input. Its stored constants, instructions and worst-case evaluation operations are counted in the same polynomial bound; it requires no further target access. This permits any such efficiently evaluable predictor, including ones outside the intersection class. All these predictors are Borel measurable.

The real-arithmetic convention explicitly fills the source’s unspecified continuous-input cost interface. Exact Gaussian coordinates need not have finite binary representations, so this branch does not silently claim an equivalent finite-bit learning theorem. Conversely the discrete branch uses actual bit costs and Boolean outputs. A result stated in a different computational model must justify the transfer before it resolves the corresponding branch. Independent programs and constants for the two branches are allowed; each program must be uniform over its own parameters.
answer_criterion: Give Lean proofs deciding the displayed uniform-existence proposition for each of \(D=\gamma\) and \(D=U\). A positive proof supplies one learner, universal polynomial constants, termination/resource bounds, a valid finite predictor and the learning guarantee for every parameter and target. A negative proof negates that full existence statement: for every candidate learner and polynomial constants, show a violating parameter/target or resource requirement. A conditional lower bound proves only the corresponding implication unless its assumption is also established. A restriction to statistical-query learners, proper hypotheses, fixed \(k\), a positive margin or a different sample source does not by itself resolve these propositions. State the model transfer for any invoked bound. The answer is a pair of exact truth values; no numerical approximation or unspecified asymptotic exponent counts as a resolution.

context_blocks.text: The selected question is in the related-work discussion of the 2025 paper. Its antecedent distributions are Gaussian inputs and the uniform Boolean cube. The original card title mentioned factorizable distributions, which describe the surrounding paper’s main two-halfspace margin theorem; that title did not describe the selected question. The revised title restores the source scope.

An individual linear inequality is a simple classifier. An intersection accepts only points satisfying every inequality, while a rejected example does not say which condition failed. The desired learner receives labeled examples and may output any efficient predictor, rather than having to reconstruct the hidden inequalities.

The 2025 paper’s main result assumes two component halfspaces, a positive data margin, and a factorization relative to the subspace of relevant directions. Those are additional promises. Its theorem therefore does not resolve the separate question about a variable number of arbitrary affine halfspaces under the two known distributions.

Alman–Patel–Servedio’s 2026 Theorem 1 learns arbitrary Boolean functions of \(k\) halfspaces from random examples under any distribution in time \(\operatorname{poly}(2^{\sqrt n(\log n)^{O(k)}},1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta))\). The paper specifically notes the previously missing subexponential bound for two halfspaces on the uniform cube at \(\varepsilon=1/n\). This is substantial progress, but the displayed bound is not polynomial in \(n,k,1/\varepsilon\).

The STOC 2026 Gaussian sparsification theorem has learning applications for intersections with bounded geometric width, meaning the defining hyperplanes have a bounded distance from the origin in its stated representation. Its constants depend on width and accuracy. That result does not supply a single polynomial bound for arbitrary thresholds and arbitrary accuracy in the current question.

The May 2026 proper agnostic learner for Gaussian functions of halfspaces also includes realizable labels as a special case. However its dimension exponent depends on the number of halfspaces and inverse error, and it has an additional parameter-dependent term. The output restriction is stronger than needed here, but the running-time guarantee does not meet the fully polynomial target.
